items.html: Quick check on one gate, then I'll write it up.

My take: the numerical core and how it's verified are very good, and probably better verified than upstream treams. The risk is everything around it. The benchmark evidence is growing faster than the library, and some of it has already gone stale.

What's strong

  • The design split is right. Rust owns the numerics and the analytic gradients behind one contract: a forward call returns an output plus a residual, and a pullback call consumes it. JAX, PyTorch and Advect just build on that. Nothing silently falls back to treams or SciPy. It's the design I'd pick for a differentiable T-matrix code.
  • The checking is unusually thorough. It includes 527 comparisons against upstream workflows, independent high-precision references, physical-invariant checks, and proptest/Hypothesis. Finite differences are only used to check results. It found real upstream defects (upstream-findings.md) and a real Mie failure at size parameter 80.
  • The reporting is honest. Slower cases, higher-memory cases and the missed 40% agent-time target are all written down, not quietly dropped.
  • It's fast and lean. The median speedup is 5× on the broad grid and 27× on size scaling, NumPy is the only runtime dependency, and unsafe is banned. The README example ran in 7 ms here.
  • The API redesign fixed a real bug class: bound field operators were applying the response twice.

What concerns me

  1. status.md is broken right now. Merge 4324000 (now f93276f) left half-resolved conflicts at status.md:34 and status.md:210. The ||||||| 2843a70 (now 7c5ae9d) markers and the old text are still there. So the doc says the benchmark campaign is complete, then that it "remains paused", and repeats the Sep 19 paragraph. just verify still passes because the pre-commit conflict check doesn't look for |||||||.
  2. The evidence is too heavy. benchmarks/ is 652 MB on disk and the git pack is 234 MiB after 75 commits. That one merge committed about 70 MB of split .tar.gz files, which now stay in history for good. status.md reads like a lab notebook (dates, commit hashes, machine specs, case counts) rather than a statement of what the library supports. For a 0.1.0 alpha, I'd keep only the current capabilities there and move the archives to release assets or LFS, with one index file pointing to them.
  3. The Python layer is as big as the Rust. There are about 15.6k lines of Python against roughly 16.3k in the Rust core plus 7.6k in the bindings. advect.py (1.8k), _framework.py (1.5k) and diff.py (1.4k) are large for adapters that are meant to be thin. I haven't read them, but that size usually means each function is wrapped by hand instead of through one shared mechanism. Also, both faer and nalgebra ship; it's worth checking whether you need both.
  4. Who is it for? It's private, has one author, is mostly agent-driven, and includes an evaluation campaign that treats agents as the users. That's fine, but the answer decides whether all the qualification work pays off. […]

What I'd do

  • Fix the two leftover conflict blocks, and add a ||||||| check to file-hygiene.
  • Decide soon where the archives should live. The longer they stay in git, the more clones carry them, and removing them later means rewriting history.
  • Split status.md into a capabilities page and a separate benchmark log.

This is based on the docs, repo structure, git history and running the README example. I didn't run just verify or read the adapter and Rust code in depth.
